newsitem.title: INDIA: India may "bundle out" notorious Sobhraj - lawyer.
newsitem.headline: India may "bundle out" notorious Sobhraj - lawyer.

text.p: India may force notorious criminal Charles Sobhraj to leave the country immediately after a crucial court appearance later this week, his lawyer said on Thursday.
Rajan Bakshi, Sobhraj's lawyer, told Reuters that he would not be surprised if the government went out of its way to expedite his client's departure. The court hearing is set for Friday.
"I think once the jail break case is dismissed they will just bundle him out of the country like they bundled him into the police van when he was released by the court," Bakshi said.

Sobhraj, whose exploits across Asia have been the basis of two books, won release from prison on Monday after more than two decades behind bars but was immediately grabbed by police outside the courtroom and detained on lack of legal documents.

Two cases are still pending in Indian courts against Sobhraj, a French citizen born to an Indian father and a Vietnamese mother. One concerns a lapsed Thai extradition request, the other stems from a 1986 jailbreak that earned Sobhraj fame.
Sobhraj would not spend more time in jail even if convicted since the maximum penalty would be less than the 11 years he has served since his escape, Bakshi said.
Bakshi said his prime concern was to ensure his client's freedom, irrespective of where he stayed.
"I think France is good for him because if he stays here (India) then he is likely to be harassed," Bakshi said.
On Tuesday the Indian government decided to drop all pending cases against Sobhraj in order to press for his speedy deportation to France.

"We have talked with the French Embassy and they said they will issue a laissez passer (transit pass) to Charles Sobhraj which would enable him to travel to France," an official at the Foreigners Regional Registration Officer (FRRO) told Reuters.
French officials in Paris confirmed that Sobhraj was free to return to France.
"All French citizens have the right to live in France," Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said.
Other French officials said Paris was prepared to provide Sobhraj with a laissez-passer facilitating his return once India issued an order to expel him.
A laissez-passer is a one-way document that would allow Sobhraj to be deported back to Paris. The temporary travel document would not allow Sobhraj to enter a third country.
Sobhraj told reporters last week that he would stay in India for some months before going to France to work on a $15 million film based on his life.

Sobhraj was first arrested in India for holding up a hotel jewellery shop in 1971. He has since been charged with a long string of crimes including murder, serving time for some and winning acquittal in others.
